_comment: Hand-picked mock OA papers. Every set was chosen problem-by-problem, not sampled: the questions ramp (Q1 is the warm-up, the last one decides the paper), no two questions in a set want the same technique, and no problem appears in two sets. Company sets use that company's own bank problems where the bank has enough of them. `minutes` is the real paper length, hand-set per set, not the sum of the estimates. AUTHORING RULE: a blurb may describe pacing, ramp and traps, but must NEVER name the technique — the app hides tags and topics on problems for exactly this reason. The two sets marked "themed" are the deliberate exception: their whole point is drilling one family, and the title says so up front.

sets.title: Microsoft — Campus Screen
sets.blurb: A short screen. Bank Q1 quickly and give the rest of the hour to Q2 — that's the one that separates candidates.

sets.title: Amazon — SDE Intern OA
sets.blurb: Two mediums and no warm-up — the intern paper opens at full difficulty. Read both before you start typing.

sets.title: Goldman Sachs — HackerRank Screen
sets.blurb: Q1 takes five minutes if you find the shortcut and forty if you don't. Q2 rewards pinning down the exact rule before writing code.

sets.title: DE Shaw — Dev Screen
sets.blurb: Both questions punish the obvious implementation: one on the size of the numbers, one on the size of the input.

sets.title: Uber — Rapid Round
sets.blurb: Both questions have a short answer once you see it. Spend the first ten minutes looking, not typing.

sets.title: Microsoft — Full OA
sets.blurb: Q1 and Q2 are bankable in forty minutes between them. Q3 will take everything you leave it, so leave it plenty.

sets.title: Amazon — SDE-1 OA
sets.blurb: Three genuine mediums and no easy question — exactly what Amazon ships. Triage matters more than depth here.

sets.title: Goldman Sachs — Pre-Superday
sets.blurb: A quick opener, then a long fiddly middle question, then one that needs a real idea. Don't let Q2 eat the paper.

sets.title: Grids & Graphs — Themed Drill
sets.blurb: Themed, so the family is no secret: three questions that are the same idea in three different costumes. The skill being drilled is recognising it the third time as fast as the first.

sets.title: Google — Coding Screen
sets.blurb: Two setup questions and one that decides the paper. Q3 is worth more than Q1 and Q2 put together.

sets.title: Flipkart — HirePro Full OA
sets.blurb: The full HirePro shape. Bank the two mediums, then pick which of Q3 and Q4 you actually intend to finish — opening Q4 with thirty minutes left is how this paper is failed.

sets.title: DE Shaw — Onsite-Level OA
sets.blurb: The hardest paper in here. Q3 and Q4 both have an obvious solution that is a hundred times too slow, and the samples won't tell you.

sets.title: Dynamic Programming — Themed Drill
sets.blurb: Themed, so the family is no secret: four questions from one family, chosen because each needs a different shape of it. If you can only do one shape, this paper will show you which.

sets.title: Mixed Bag — Generic Product OA
sets.blurb: What most three-hour papers actually look like: four unrelated questions, one of them considerably nastier than it first reads.

sets.title: Citadel — Quant Dev OA
sets.blurb: Tight constraints throughout. Every question here has a solution that passes the samples and dies on the real tests — check your complexity against the limits before you submit.
